proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I tell myself I'll sort my finances when I earn more?"
description: "You said it at £30k. You said it at £50k. The number changed. The feeling didn't. Here's what's actually going on."
pubDate: "2026-08-26"
tags: ["money worship", "behavioural money", "earning more"]
---

You said it at £30k. You'll get on top of it when you hit £40k.

Then £40k arrived, lifestyle adjusted within about three months, and you said it again.

There's a version of this that's just maths: income rose, fixed costs rose with it, not much slack appeared. That part is real. But it's not the whole story, because some people on your salary are building something and you know it.

The harder thing to sit with is this: at some point the "when I earn more" framing stopped being a plan and started being a way of not looking too closely at now.

Joel went through a version of this himself. MSc in behavioural economics, qualified financial planner, a career spent helping other people think clearly about money. He still found himself with a tax return tab he hadn't opened in six weeks sitting in a browser he used every day. The knowledge was there. The looking was the problem.

That gap between knowing and doing is not a discipline failure. It's information. It's telling you something about what the money means to you, and what you're afraid the numbers might confirm.

The question worth asking is not "how do I earn more." It's "what am I expecting more money to fix that more money has never actually fixed."

That's the thing worth turning toward. Not because it's comfortable, but because the current approach has a track record you can already measure.

If you want to understand what's underneath the pattern, [take the money psychology quiz](#). It takes four minutes and it won't tell you anything you don't already half-know.
